name: Radial longitudinal deficiency (radial club hand)
aliases: preaxial deficiency of the upper limb

reference.source: Green's Operative Hand Surgery / Tachdjian's Pediatric Orthopaedics
clinicalPearls: Represents a spectrum of preaxial (radial-side) failure of formation, ranging from a mildly hypoplastic thumb to complete absence of the radius with the hand deviated radially at the wrist
The forearm is usually short and bowed, the unsupported carpus deviates radially (the 'club hand' appearance), and the thumb is frequently hypoplastic or absent
Severity is graded (Bayne and later modifications) from a deficient distal radial epiphysis through partial to complete radial aplasia, incorporating thumb and carpal deficiency
Strong systemic associations mandate a syndrome search: VACTERL association, Fanconi anaemia, thrombocytopenia-absent-radius (TAR) syndrome, and Holt-Oram (heart-hand) syndrome
Because Fanconi anaemia and TAR carry haematological risk, screening (chromosomal breakage testing and a full blood count) is essential before any surgery
Early treatment centres on stretching and splinting to correct wrist alignment, with surgical centralisation or radialisation of the carpus over the ulna reserved for suitable cases
Thumb reconstruction by pollicisation of the index finger restores pinch when the thumb is absent or non-functional
reference.pathophysiology: The deformity arises from failure of formation along the preaxial (radial) margin of the developing upper limb bud in early gestation, affecting the radius, radial carpal bones, thumb ray, and the associated muscles, radial nerve, and vessels. The degree of radial deficiency determines the radial deviation of the hand and the instability of the wrist, as the carpus loses its bony support. Because the same limb-patterning and progenitor pathways influence blood formation and cardiac development, radial longitudinal deficiency is frequently part of systemic disorders affecting haematopoiesis (Fanconi anaemia, thrombocytopenia-absent-radius) or the heart (Holt-Oram syndrome), which must always be sought.
additionalDifferentials: Isolated thumb hypoplasia without radial deficiency
Cleft hand or central longitudinal deficiency
Constriction ring (amniotic band) sequence affecting the forearm
Acquired radial deficiency following trauma, infection, or tumour resection
additionalInvestigations: Radiographs of the whole upper limb to grade radial, carpal, and thumb deficiency
Full blood count and blood film to screen for thrombocytopenia (TAR syndrome)
Chromosomal breakage testing (diepoxybutane or mitomycin C) to exclude Fanconi anaemia before surgery
Echocardiography and cardiology review for Holt-Oram or VACTERL cardiac anomalies
Renal ultrasound and spinal radiographs as part of VACTERL screening
Genetic assessment with karyotyping or targeted gene testing
redFlags: Undiagnosed Fanconi anaemia, which can progress to marrow failure and malignancy if missed before surgery
Severe thrombocytopenia in TAR syndrome risking perioperative haemorrhage
Associated cardiac or renal anomalies (Holt-Oram or VACTERL) needing evaluation before anaesthesia
Bilateral severe deformity with limited elbow extension compromising hand-to-mouth function
reference.prognosis: With appropriate splinting, centralisation, and pollicisation, function and appearance improve substantially, but recurrence of radial deviation and continued forearm shortening are common as the child grows; the overall outlook is heavily influenced by any underlying syndrome, particularly the haematological disorders.
pitfalls: Treating the hand deformity without screening for Fanconi anaemia or TAR, thereby missing a life-threatening haematological disorder
Overlooking associated cardiac, renal, or vertebral anomalies
Performing aggressive centralisation when elbow extension is limited, which can worsen function by preventing hand-to-mouth movement
Neglecting thumb function, which is often more disabling than the wrist deformity itself
